falsification_conditions: Fatal for the narrow hardware-resale thesis if three to five independently recruited Chilean businesses will not pay at or below the prevailing CLP 10,000–25,000 market range for a configured display.

Fatal if landed unit economics show less than approximately 30% contribution margin before founder sales time, or if fulfillment and configuration take more than 20 minutes per unit without a compensating setup fee.
Fatal if a seven- to fourteen-day pilot across at least five businesses produces no measurable scans or taps despite visible placement and staff consent.
Fatal if businesses report that existing QR signage, Google links, staff requests, or incumbent vendors solve the problem at zero or negligible incremental cost and they reject replacement.

Fatal for a review-focused positioning if buyers object to asking for reviews, if venues cannot place the display at the point of service, or if the product creates review-policy or reputational concerns.

Fatal for scale if customer acquisition depends on bespoke in-person selling and repeatable paid acquisition cannot be demonstrated at a customer-acquisition cost below first-order contribution profit.
Fatal for recurring software claims if at least ten paying businesses decline analytics, destination management, or reporting after receiving a working hardware product.

The thesis should be downgraded if observed interactions do not translate into completed reviews or contacts, or if any apparent uplift cannot be compared with a documented pre-pilot baseline or control period.
cards.judgment: A legitimate, identifiable physical product and buyer job exist: configured NFC-plus-QR review/contact displays for checkout, reception, and table-service settings. Chilean competitors, published pricing, nationwide delivery, and at least some marketplace sales establish real availability, competition, and limited buyer acceptance. However, this is not yet HQ-worthy as a distribution business because the proposed entrant has no evidenced supplier terms, landed-cost model, after-sales/replacement plan, or defensible differentiation versus established local sellers. The inexpensive paid pilot is appropriate, but it must test willingness to buy from a new provider and contribution economics, not merely usage of free/discounted signage.
next_validation_questions: Unit landed cost for blank NFC tags, acrylic or printed displays, packaging, and Chilean delivery.

Incremental tap rate, QR scan rate, completed review rate, and repeat usage by venue type and placement.
Whether review prompts produce sustainable incremental reviews rather than merely redirecting customers who would have reviewed anyway.
cards.participation_path: Lowest-cost falsification: buy or make 3–5 low-cost NFC/QR displays using the publicly listed CLP 9,990–19,990 price range, configure each to a distinct review or contact destination, and run a seven-day pilot with independently recruited local businesses that consent to placement. Record scans/taps, completed review actions and staff-observed usage; do not claim incremental reviews unless the business shares a before/after baseline. Offer the pilot first as a paid purchase at or below the observed local price, or as a refundable trial only if the business agrees in writing. Stop if no business agrees to place the display or no measurable interactions occur.
cards.thesis: The generic NFC-card market is already served, so an independent operator should not compete on ordinary networking cards. A narrower offer is a configured, location-specific review/contact display for businesses where staff can prompt a customer at checkout, reception or table service. The verifiable purchase prices establish customer willingness to pay for the hardware, but do not establish conversion uplift or recurring software willingness to pay.

contrary_evidence:
There is genuine regulatory complexity that could create demand. SEC identifies RGR N°06/2024 as the technical instruction for battery energy-storage systems, and the published document covers BESS composition and technical requirements. SEC also maintains formal product-authorization and TE4 declaration systems, including public visibility into rejected or inscrita filings. These facts support the existence of a compliance workflow and potential error-reduction value, but they do not establish that an independent pre-check is required or monetizable. Sources: https://www.sec.cl/sitio-web/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/RGR-N-06-2024_v4.pdf ; https://wlhttp.sec.cl/productManager/login ; https://wlhttp.sec.cl/edeclaradorTE4/usuarioPublicoERNC.do

SEC's public installer-search system explicitly includes review of installations and preparation of electrical projects among installer work categories, which is contrary evidence to the assumption that installers lack review capability. Source: https://wlhttp.sec.cl/buscadorinstaladores/buscador.do

The regulatory framework appears active rather than static: SEC lists later modifications to the distributed-generation instructions and current public consultation or training activity. This supports a need for monitoring, but also increases product-maintenance burden and the risk that a low-priced checklist cannot remain accurate. falsification_conditions: At least 8 of 10 qualified target installers state that they already perform the relevant review internally and would not pay for an external pre-check.
Three consecutive qualified prospects decline to provide a redacted equipment list or cannot identify a recent compliance-related delay, rejection, or rework cost.
A paid pilot produces no specific, nontrivial gap that the installer accepts as useful, or the installer would not rely on the output even as an internal review aid.

A licensed Chilean electrical professional or SEC communication indicates that the proposed service would require authorization the operator does not possess, or that the checklist could be misleading without regulated sign-off.
The applicable SEC or distributor process does not require the claimed AFCI, product-authorization, or documentation checks for the targeted project segment.

Prospects will only accept the service bundled with installation, engineering, certification, or submission responsibility that the operator cannot legally or operationally provide.

A competing installer, vendor, certification body, or public SEC tool provides the same review at no incremental cost and prospects identify no meaningful difference in speed, accuracy, or accountability.
cards.judgment: This is a plausible Chile-specific compliance-services research wedge rather than an energy-asset investment thesis. Primary SEC materials support that BESS/distributed-generation compliance and authorized-installer processes exist, and the proposed payer is identifiable: authorized installers/EPCs or project owners facing filing and equipment-documentation risk. The service can likely be scoped as non-certifying document review, so unattainable interconnection or asset-custody requirements are not established. However, it is not yet HQ-worthy as a survivor: there is no evidence of relevant BESS project volume, rejection/rework incidence, avoided-cost magnitude, willingness to pay, legal scope for an unlicensed reviewer, or a durable advantage over installers, engineers, vendors, and SEC tools. It also does not itself demonstrate a price, capacity, reliability, or power-electronics investment edge; it is an ancillary service whose demand depends on those projects occurring. Advance only as tightly bounded customer-discovery and legal-scope research, not as a bankable opportunity or standalone energy-infrastructure investment.
next_validation_questions: Whether the cited January 1, 2026 AFCI requirement applies to the exact project classes, inverter configurations, and connection pathways targeted by the product, rather than only specified cases or alternatives.

cards.participation_path: Use the SEC's public installer and technical-documentation pages to identify 10 authorized distributed-generation installers. Send a one-page sample checklist covering RGR N°06/2024, AFCI status, equipment authorization and required filing fields. Ask whether they would pay for one review of a real but anonymized project, without promising approval. Test with one paid or explicitly unpaid pilot only after the installer confirms the scope. Falsify if installers report that they already perform the review internally, will not share a redacted equipment list, or do not value error reduction enough to accept a trial. Do not install, certify or submit electrical work without the required authorization.
cards.thesis: A narrow, testable asset is a paid pre-check package for installers or project owners: collect equipment datasheets, compare the proposed battery/PCE/inverter configuration against the current SEC checklist, identify missing AFCI or documentation items, and produce a submission-ready gap list. The mechanism is avoided rework or rejected filings, not speculative battery arbitrage. The operator must avoid representing itself as an authorized electrical installer unless it actually has that authorization.

contrary_evidence: There is genuine evidence that the underlying supply exists: VIC Robotics publicly describes RaaS beginning at UF 20/month, with installation, mapping, maintenance, hardware replacement, software updates, and local support included. Robotic Work states that it is an official PUDU distributor in Chile and has local technical capacity and spare parts. Dimacofi separately markets PUDU cleaning equipment with national support. cards.judgment: The underlying industrial-floor-cleaning use case is identifiable and local Chilean supply/support appears plausibly available through several distributors, so this is not yet fatally blocked by an unidentifiable buyer or practical pilot barrier. However, it does not survive as an HQ-worthy business case yet: the proposed intermediary has no written, compensable channel role; published RaaS starting prices do not establish site-level unit economics; and there is no independent, comparable evidence of labor displacement, throughput/quality improvement, uptime, or intervention burden in a Chilean target facility. The opportunity is therefore a tightly bounded validation hypothesis, not a validated distribution, leasing, or managed-operation business.

falsification_conditions: After screening at least 20 qualified commercial leads, fewer than three installers agree to a paid or recurring pilot, or no customer pays for the service.

cards.geography: Chile, initially regions with high solar generation and constrained distribution capacity
cards.judgment: This is a plausible, narrow Chile-specific service wedge rather than an investable solar/storage asset thesis: SEC’s distributed-generation platforms, installer requirements, equipment information, and preliminary low-voltage-capacity data provide a real regulatory/workflow substrate for prequalification. The proposed payer types are identifiable—SEC-authorized installers or small-commercial customers—and the service can be falsified cheaply before making any operating commitment. However, no named off-taker, installer, or paying customer has been validated; willingness to pay, repeatability, liability allocation, and unit economics are all unresolved. It should survive only as research into whether prequalification reduces installer sales-engineering cost or improves conversion enough to support a paid subcontract, not as evidence that solar-plus-storage projects themselves have attractive economics.
next_validation_questions: Whether small Chilean businesses will pay directly for a pre-feasibility report rather than obtain a free installer quote.

cards.participation_path: Use the SEC authorized-installer directory as a distribution list. The lowest-cost falsification test is to complete five screenings manually, without buying equipment or promising installation, and measure whether at least one installer or customer requests a paid follow-up. cards.thesis: A small operator can reduce failed site visits and non-viable proposals by screening a customer’s load profile, roof/site, equipment eligibility, and preliminary network capacity before an authorized installer prepares a formal installation and connection proposal. cards.judgment: Survives as an HQ-worthy, narrowly framed research/watchlist hypothesis—not an investment thesis—because it uses dated SEC-source evidence, names accessible listed-company candidates, distinguishes awarded/contracted backlog from realized economics, and defines observable falsification tests. However, no valuation-versus-risked-value work, per-share dilution analysis, or liquidity verification is provided, so it cannot yet support a governed investment decision. The three issuers also have materially different economics: WESCO is a leveraged distributor with working-capital and margin exposure; ERock has unusually large backlog relative to current revenue and apparent customer/order-conversion concentration; Ameresco's data-center projects have long-dated 2028–2032 execution, financing, permitting, interconnection, and capital-intensity risk. The stated catalyst is therefore not a near-term common basket catalyst, and much of the demand news may already be reflected in market expectations.

evidence.claim: The IEA reports that more than 2,500 GW of renewable, storage and large-load projects are stalled in grid queues and that annual grid investment may need to rise roughly 50% by 2030 from about $400 billion today.

falsification_conditions: By 2028, major U.S. power markets consistently connect new hyperscale data centers within roughly 24 to 36 months without material firm-capacity premiums or persistent transmission constraints.
AI energy efficiency improves sufficiently that global data-center electricity demand grows materially below current IEA projections despite continued user and revenue growth.
A sustained wave of data-center cancellations, load reductions, or utilization shortfalls causes regional load forecasts to be revised downward for at least two consecutive years.
Interconnection-queue reform, transmission expansion, flexible-load standards, or utility investment reduces connection backlogs and congestion costs without creating durable scarcity rents.
The majority of commercial deployments in generation, storage, demand response, cooling, procurement, and interconnection software fail to earn returns above the cost of capital.
Independent evidence shows that most claimed grid bottlenecks are temporary construction or permitting delays rather than durable constraints on delivered power.
Hyperscalers primarily solve power needs internally or through long-term bilateral contracts, leaving insufficient third-party gross margin for the proposed solution categories.
cards.geography: global, with pronounced effects in the United States and other advanced power markets
cards.judgment: The underlying premise is well grounded by recent IEA and regulatory/market sources: data-center load growth and constrained interconnection/transmission capacity can make delivered, reliable power and time-to-connection economically important. There are identifiable payers—hyperscalers, colocation operators, utilities, and large industrial loads—and credible value pools. However, this is a macro condition rather than a sufficiently specified opportunity. It bundles capital-intensive generation and storage with regulated grid technologies and software/services, each with different buyers, margins, sales cycles, approvals, and competitive dynamics. A generic participation path is plausible, but no particular constrained node, customer segment, product wedge, economics, capital requirement, or defensible advantage is identified. It merits targeted research to isolate a narrow, capital-efficient wedge; it is not yet an HQ-ready investment or operating thesis.
next_validation_questions: Whether AI demand, revenue, and utilization will grow fast enough to offset rapid reductions in energy per task.

cards.participation_path: Target constrained power markets with grid-flexibility or connection bottlenecks; sell capacity, optimization or interconnection solutions to data centers, utilities and industrial users; evaluate projects using delivered power and time-to-connection rather than compute price alone.
cards.thesis: The scarce input for AI and digital infrastructure is increasingly not only compute hardware but also reliable, rapidly connectable power and transmission capacity. This changes site selection, financing, project timelines and the economics of flexible or distributed generation.

cards.judgment: Primary CMF sources in the supplied provenance support that Chile’s SFA has published technical implementation material, a developer environment, a July 2027 phased entry-into-force target, and the ATENA sandbox. cards.judgment: The regulatory premise is well grounded by primary European Commission sources: Article 50 transparency obligations and the relevant enforcement framework became operational on 2 August 2026. A viable participation path likely requires a sharply differentiated wedge—e.g., cross-provider evidence trails, workflow-specific compliance automation, independent assurance, or regulated-sector implementation—not generic provenance/watermarking or broad 'AI Act compliance' tooling. cards.judgment: The underlying regulatory change is supported by primary CMF sources in the provided provenance, so this is not rejected for an unverified or misread regulatory premise. A narrowly scoped, customer-authorized readiness assessment is legally plausible: it can rely on public CMF materials and a prospective participant’s own technical environment rather than requiring independent access to protected financial data. The July 2027 effective date and heterogeneous participant obligations also weaken immediate urgency. Treat this only as HQ-worthy research into one exact buyer/flow—e.g., a regulated payment-data participant needing consent-flow and field-mapping remediation—not as a general open-finance implementation business.

cards.judgment: This is a research-survivor watchlist thesis, not an investable conclusion. It names a liquid public security exposure (Powell Industries/POWL, with SEC-filed disclosures) and offers dated, primary-source demand indicators: $1.8 billion backlog at March 31, 2026 and a subsequently disclosed data-center order exceeding $400 million. The proposed mechanism—conversion of equipment backlog into revenue, margin, cash flow, and ultimately valuation—is falsifiable and has a plausible 12- to 18-month operating-catalyst window, with liquidity available through public shares. However, the record does not establish the essential valuation comparison: no share price, enterprise value, earnings/cash-flow expectations, backlog valuation, downside case, or relative valuation versus capable competitors is supplied. It also does not substantiate customer credit, contract firmness, cancellation terms, funding, margin profile, working-capital needs, or the portion of Powell backlog actually attributable to data centers. The evidence supports genuine demand and a monitorable catalyst, but not a demonstrated public-market mispricing or asymmetric expected-return case. No fatal condition is triggered because the thesis does not rely on a post-hoc chart, assert 10x upside, use promotional metrics as dispositive evidence, or propose an unavailable vehicle.

cards.judgment: The regulatory and infrastructure signal is sufficiently grounded in CMF primary materials: the SFA technical framework and ATENA sandbox support the conclusion that implementation/interoperability work is moving forward, so this is not rejected for an unverified regulatory change. cards.judgment: Chile’s Open Finance direction and standardized account-data API documentation are sufficiently grounded in CMF primary materials to support research. The cited account APIs indicate that regulated, consent-based access is technically contemplated, so this is not presently disproven by an unavailable-data/API fatal condition. However, the commercial proposition is an infrastructure-level migration thesis rather than a defined business with demonstrated ability to capture value. The payment-initiation material is described as a consultation/process item, and the supplied record itself identifies a delayed, phased path toward July 2027 and beyond; it should not be treated as immediate, stable production access. A new entrant also faces potentially material licensing, security, consent, privacy, AML, operational-resilience, certification, and dispute-handling obligations. Those costs may be rational for a focused, regulated use case with proprietary distribution or risk/workflow advantage, but there is no evidence yet that standalone aggregation/orchestration economics justify them. The proposed research question is appropriately falsifiable: whether a concentrated, long-duration backlog converts into revenue, cash flow, and per-share value. cards.judgment: The cited U.S. SEC filings credibly support that tokenized-fund operations can require wallet allowlists, reconciliation to authoritative transfer-agent records, transfer controls, and audit evidence. A non-production synthetic test harness could avoid directly performing custody, KYC, transfer-agent, or securities activity, so legal/API impossibility is not established. cards.participation_path: Select one local facility type and compile a list of publicly identifiable sites with large hard-floor areas. Send a factual one-page pilot brief referencing the provider’s published RaaS price and request permission to forward the inquiry to the provider. Run one no-cost discovery call or site walk only after the facility expresses interest; stop if no facility agrees to discuss floor area, cleaning labor, or a pilot. Do not represent the provider, promise savings, or purchase a robot without written authorization.
cards.thesis: The offer creates a concrete procurement and pilot mechanism for warehouses, supermarkets, offices, clinics, and hotels that may prefer a monthly operating expense over capital purchase. The evidence verifies an available offer, not unmet demand or customer savings.
cards.title: Warehouse-cleaning robot pilot sold as an operating expense
cards.value_capture_mechanism: Participate as a site-identification and pilot coordinator only if the provider accepts referrals or a target facility requests an introduction. A small operator could also sell a paid site-measurement or cleaning-route feasibility study, but no buyer, referral fee, or margin was verified.

cards.geography: Chile, especially Coquimbo and central agricultural regions
next_validation_questions: Identify a real buyer, purchasing trigger, distribution route and net unit economics.
cards.participation_path: Partner with one local irrigation installer or farm to instrument a single block using low-cost flow meters, soil-moisture readings, and manual crop/output records; compare against a nearby untreated block where feasible. Lowest-cost falsification: obtain permission for a 2-4 week baseline measurement before proposing equipment or software, and ask the partner to specify the decision the measurement would change. Stop if no operator will provide site access, baseline records, or a decision deadline.
cards.thesis: A narrow, testable offer is field measurement and ROI verification for one irrigation retrofit or water-saving production practice, rather than a broad smart-farming platform. The economic mechanism is helping a producer or installer document water use, crop performance, and payback for an existing investment or grant/procurement decision.
cards.title: Water-efficiency field validation service for Chilean irrigated agriculture
cards.value_capture_mechanism: Potential payment from a farm, irrigation installer, exporter, agricultural cooperative, or technology supplier for a small baseline-and-follow-up measurement project. No savings, buyer, or subsidy eligibility is assumed.
